appraisal_events.evidence: « je l'ai trouvé curieux. Je ne l'ai pas trouvé simple ! Mais il a quelque chose d'amusant, d'" obtenu " [...] une chose qui m'étonne et ne me plaît pas infiniment » ; « il a sur les œuvres d'art un goût en quelque sorte infaillible, il ne se trompe jamais ; si quelque chose est beau, il le reconnaît tout de suite, il le prend en haine » ; « (Tout le monde sourit.) »
appraisal_events.explanation: The table jointly demolishes the Emperor as a person and as a judge of art: Mme de Guermantes delivers a fastidious verdict (curious, not simple, artificially "obtenu" like a green carnation), and the prince Von, instead of defending his sovereign, converts the formal praise of his "infallible" taste into a joke that his judgment is reliably inverted, a demolition the whole company ratifies by smiling and the princesse by saying she is reassured.

appraisal_events.evidence: « reprit le prince qui, ne sachant pas prononcer le mot archéologue (c'est-à-dire comme si c'était écrit kéologue), ne perdait jamais une occasion de s'en servir » ; « et le prince dit arshéologue »
appraisal_events.explanation: While the prince is scoring his witticism, the narrator quietly ridicules him by noting that he cannot pronounce the word "archéologue" and therefore never misses a chance to use it, and by transcribing "arshéologue" four times, so that his display of cultivated irony is itself framed as comic pretension.

status_effects.explanation: The Emperor is clearly diminished in this exchange: judged artificial and unpleasing by Mme de Guermantes, then turned by his own subject into an infallible negative barometer of artistic worth, to the amusement of the whole table.
He takes over the conversation with a sustained, well-received joke that defuses the duchesse's risky criticism of his sovereign, wins the table's smile and draws the princesse's "Vous me rassurez".
The narrator's aside about his mispronounced, compulsively repeated "arshéologue" undercuts the same performance, making him locally ridiculous even as he is socially successful.

Her italicized "obtenu"/green-carnation verdict is staged as a performed mot that sets the terms of the exchange; her daring criticism of an emperor before his own subject is not rebuked but accommodated and extended.

ambiguities: The referent of « lui »/« il » in the duchesse's speech is read here as the Emperor, not Elstir: her « Oui » answers the prince's immediately preceding « L'empereur est d'une merveilleuse intelligence », the German-linked hostesses (tante Sagan, tante Radziwill) fit the Emperor, and « J'espère que je ne vous " choque " pas ? » only makes sense as fear of offending the German prince about his sovereign, whose works of Elstir he has just said he does not know. The alternative reading (Elstir) would move the target of E1.

Speakers are designated only by pronoun or title: « elle » is resolved to the duchesse de Guermantes (the italicizing-by-pronunciation mannerism the narrator has just described as hers, plus the aristocratic aunts and the wit), « la princesse » to the princesse de Parme, the ranking guest at this dinner, and « le prince » to the prince Von, named a few paragraphs earlier — not the prince de Guermantes, who is discussed at this dinner as absent.
